title: Hiking in Snowdonia
strapline: From Snowdon's bustling paths to the raw wilderness of the Rhinogs, Snowdonia hiking delivers proper adventure.
metaDescription: Discover the best hiking in Snowdonia National Park. Explore trails, tips, routes, and gear advice for your Snowdonia adventure.
heroAlt: Hikers on a rocky summit overlooking a dramatic Snowdonia valley.
introduction:
Snowdonia. Eryri. Call it what you will, this corner of North Wales is a hiker's paradise, no arguments. Forget manicured trails and gentle strolls; here, the mountains bite back. We're talking proper peaks, scrambling ridges, and views that'll stop you dead in your tracks. 

Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon) inevitably hogs the limelight, and rightly so — six different routes offer varying levels of challenge, from the relatively gentle Llanberis Path to the exposed Crib Goch, a knife-edge arete only for those with a head for heights. But Snowdon is one of fifteen Welsh peaks over 3,000ft, and the wilder ranges are where the park actually opens up. Tryfan's North Ridge is the classic Grade 1 scramble. The Glyderau Bochlwyd Horseshoe links Tryfan with Glyder Fach and Glyder Fawr via Bristly Ridge and the Cantilever Stone — a lunar landscape of shattered rock found nowhere else in Britain. North across the A5, the Carneddau roll on for miles: Carnedd Llewelyn and Dafydd are the second and third highest peaks in Wales, and the high plateau between them is the closest thing to genuine wilderness left in the park. Moel Siabod's Daear Ddu ridge gives you the best front-row view of the Snowdon Horseshoe you'll get from anywhere. And if you want to throw down a gauntlet, the Welsh 3000s — all fifteen 3,000-footers in a single push — is the test the serious mountain people measure themselves against. Cadair Idris, down in the south, is a quieter day with Cardigan Bay laid out below the summit.

Hiking in Snowdonia isn't always a walk in the park (literally). The weather can change in an instant, navigation can be tricky, and some routes demand serious scrambling skills. But that's the appeal, right? This is a place to test yourself, to earn those summit views, and to refuel with a well-deserved pint in a cosy pub afterwards. It's best suited for those with a decent level of fitness and some experience of hill walking. Beginners can find plenty of easier trails, but even those should be approached with respect. Come prepared, respect the mountains, and Snowdonia will reward you with memories that last a lifetime. Just remember to pack your waterproofs… and maybe a compass.
topTips: Pen-y-Pass car park now runs on a pre-booking system (via JustPark) through 1 November 2026 — an 8-hour session starts at £25 and card/contactless only, no cash. If you're heading for the Pyg Track, Miners' Track, or Crib Goch, book your slot before you drive up, not when you arrive.

Can't get a Pen-y-Pass booking? Park at Llanberis or the Nant Peris Park & Ride and take the Snowdon Sherpa bus instead — a day return to Pen-y-Pass is a few pounds and removes the parking gamble entirely. It also means you don't have to do an out-and-back on the same trail.

Every trailhead car park in this guide fills before 8am in summer — Llanberis, Ogwen Cottage, Pen-y-Pass. If you're not there for sunrise, plan on a Sherpa bus, a walk-in from a further layby, or a different, quieter route altogether.

The summit visitor centre, Hafod Eryri, only opens roughly May to late October, and only when the train is running — high wind closes it even in season. Don't count on shelter, food, or toilets at the top outside those months or on a rough-weather day.

Scrambling routes — Crib Goch, Tryfan North Ridge, Bristly Ridge on the Glyderau Horseshoe, Daear Ddu on Moel Siabod — turn from straightforward to genuinely dangerous the moment the rock gets wet or icy. If in doubt, bail to an easier line; several of these spots have a walkable alternative described in their insider tips.

Check MWIS (Mountain Weather Information Service) the night before and the morning of any highlevel walk, not just the general Met Office forecast — summit conditions in Snowdonia routinely diverge wildly from what's happening in the valley.
Weekday visits change everything here. The same routes that are nose-to-tail on a August Saturday — Llanberis Path, Crib Goch, Cwm Idwal — are genuinely peaceful on a Tuesday, even in peak season.

For remoter routes like Rhinog Fawr and the Carneddau plateau, download an offline map before you leave signal — mobile coverage disappears fast once you're off the main Snowdon massif, and the terrain on the Rhinogs in particular has few clear paths to navigate by eye.

firstTimer: Start with the Llanberis Path or Cwm Idwal Circular before attempting anything with scrambling — both give you a genuine Snowdonia day out without needing rope-free climbing skills.
Hiking boots with ankle support are non-negotiable, not a nice-to-have. The rocky, uneven terrain on almost every route here — even the 'easy' ones — will punish trainers.
Pack full waterproofs (jacket and trousers) even if the forecast at sea level looks fine. Conditions at altitude in Snowdonia can be a different world to what's happening in the car park.

Tell someone your planned route and expected return time before you set off, and stick to it. If things go wrong, mountain rescue need to know where to start looking — call 999 and ask for Mountain Rescue.
Budget more time than you think: the Llanberis Path alone is 5-6 hours round trip, and that's the easy route. Start early to give yourself daylight margin, especially outside midsummer.

Don't attempt Crib Goch, Tryfan's North Ridge, or the Glyderau Horseshoe as your first Snowdonia outing — these are exposed grade 1 scrambles that need prior experience and comfort with heights, not a first-timer's warm-up.
Bring more water and food than feels necessary. There's nowhere to refill on most routes, and Hafod Eryri at the Snowdon summit is only open roughly May–October and only when the train's running.

If you're driving to a trailhead, have a backup plan. Llanberis, Ogwen Cottage, and Pen-y-Pass car parks all fill before 8am on summer weekends — know the nearest Sherpa bus stop or Park & Ride as your Plan B.
regular: Book Pen-y-Pass parking in advance on JustPark if you're doing Crib Goch, the Pyg Track, or the Miners' Track — the car park is pre-booking only through 1 November 2026 and walking up on spec is a wasted trip.

Skip Snowdon entirely on a summer weekend and head for Moel Siabod's Daear Ddu ridge instead — you get arguably the best view of the Snowdon Horseshoe in the whole park, with a fraction of the foot traffic.

The Carneddau (Carnedd Llewelyn and Dafydd from Ogwen) is the closest thing to genuine wilderness solitude left in Snowdonia — even in peak season you'll see a fraction of the people you would on the Snowdon massif.
For scrambling days, go up Bristly Ridge on the Glyderau Horseshoe, not down — it's markedly safer in that direction, and the same logic applies to most grade 1 scrambles in the park.

Rhinog Fawr rewards those with solid navigation: there's barely a path in places, so it stays quiet even when Snowdon and the Glyderau are heaving. Bring a compass and an offline GPS track, not just a phone signal.

Nantlle Ridge is the local's alternative to the busier ridge walks — similar exposure and scrambling to routes like Crib Goch's approach, similar views, but nowhere near the crowds. Start early to beat both heat and any midday cloud building on the tops.
Off-peak midweek trips in late May or September get you the best combination Snowdonia offers: long daylight, drier rock than winter, and noticeably thinner crowds than July-August weekends.

For an easier but still scenic day when the main summits are socked in with cloud, Aber Falls into the Carneddau foothills stays walkable and rewarding even in poor visibility higher up — a good fallback rather than forcing a summit bid in bad conditions.

spots.name: Snowdon via the Llanberis Path
spots.description: The most popular and arguably easiest route to the summit of Snowdon. A well-maintained but long and steady climb suitable for beginners with good fitness. Expect crowds, especially in summer. The views from the top are unparalleled on a clear day, stretching across Snowdonia, Anglesey, and beyond.
spots.bestFor: Beginners and families looking to summit Snowdon
spots.notSuitableFor: Those seeking solitude or a challenging scramble
spots.parking: Llanberis village car parks. Pay and display, fills up very early (before 8am in summer). Park & Ride available from Nant Peris.
spots.insiderTip: Avoid weekends and school holidays. Consider starting very early or very late to avoid the crowds.
spots.howToDoIt: Follow the path from the Victoria Terrace end of Llanberis village, tracking the route of the Snowdon Mountain Railway most of the way up. It's a steady, well-graded ascent with no scrambling or route-finding required — just distance and altitude. The path is easy to follow even in poor visibility since it stays close to the railway line for much of the climb. Pace yourself on the lower slopes; the final push past the Finger Stone to the summit ridge is the steepest section.
spots.access: Start directly from Llanberis village, no walk-in needed. The path is a public right of way throughout. Parking is in the village's pay-and-display car parks, which fill by mid-morning in summer; the Nant Peris Park & Ride plus Snowdon Sherpa bus is the reliable backup once they're full.
spots.routeDescription: A steady out-and-back along the north-west flank of Snowdon, broadly shadowing the Snowdon Mountain Railway. From Llanberis, the path climbs gradually past Halfway House café, continues up open moorland, then joins the other summit routes near the top for the final rocky pull to the trig point. Return the same way, or descend via the Pyg Track/Miners' Track if you've arranged transport back to Llanberis.

spots.name: Tryfan North Ridge
spots.description: A classic grade 1 scramble up the iconic Tryfan. Requires a good head for heights and some scrambling experience. The route is exposed and rocky, demanding careful footwork. Summit views are spectacular, encompassing the Ogwen Valley and the Glyderau.
spots.bestFor: Experienced scramblers and those seeking an adrenaline rush
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners, those with a fear of heights, or in wet/icy conditions
spots.parking: Laybys along the A5 in the Ogwen Valley. Fills up very early.
spots.insiderTip: Practice on easier scrambles first. Descending via the South Ridge is generally considered safer.
spots.howToDoIt: From Ogwen Cottage, cross the road and head up the obvious path toward Tryfan's north face. The ridge proper starts with a short, easy scramble that steepens quickly — hands-on-rock throughout, with the famous summit boulders Adam and Eve (a leap between them is a rite of passage, entirely optional) marking the top. This is unroped scrambling: solid three points of contact, testing holds before committing, and a head for exposure are all essential rather than nice-to-haves. Many first-timers hire a guide or go with an experienced scrambling partner for their first ascent.
spots.access: No permit needed; Tryfan sits on open-access mountain land. Park in the laybys along the A5 through the Ogwen Valley — these are notorious for filling before 8am on any clear-weather weekend, so an early start isn't optional, it's the only way to get a space.
spots.routeDescription: The North Ridge climbs directly from the valley floor near Ogwen Cottage, gaining height fast over a series of rock steps and short walls with only intermittent path to follow — much of the route is a case of picking the best line up the ridge crest. It tops out at the twin summit boulders. Most parties descend via the easier South Ridge toward Bwlch Tryfan rather than reversing the North Ridge.

spots.name: Crib Goch
spots.description: Not for the faint of heart! Crib Goch is a notorious knife-edge arete offering exhilarating but highly exposed scrambling. Requires a very steady head for heights and excellent scrambling skills. Should only be attempted in good weather conditions. It is part of the full Snowdon Horseshoe.
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners, families, or anyone with a fear of heights. Avoid in wet, windy, or icy conditions.
spots.parking: Pen-y-Pass car park. Expensive and fills up ridiculously early (before 7am in summer).
spots.insiderTip: Consider starting very early or attempting it mid-week to avoid crowds. Check weather conditions meticulously.
spots.howToDoIt: From Pen-y-Pass, follow the Pyg Track a short way before branching up onto Crib Goch's east ridge. The ascent is a steep, hands-on scramble to the pinnacle, followed by the arete itself — an exposed, narrow ridge with severe drops on both sides where careful, deliberate movement matters far more than speed. Most parties then continue over Crib y Ddysgl to Yr Wyddfa's summit and descend via the Pyg or Miners' Track to complete the full Snowdon Horseshoe, rather than reversing the ridge.
spots.access: Open-access mountain terrain, no permit required, but Pen-y-Pass car park now runs a mandatory pre-booking system (via JustPark) through 1 November 2026 — turning up without a booking means no parking. The Snowdon Sherpa bus from Llanberis or the Nant Peris Park & Ride is the practical alternative if you can't get a slot.
spots.routeDescription: The ridge climbs steeply from Pen-y-Pass to the exposed knife-edge arete, crosses several rock pinnacles requiring careful hand and foot placement, then continues over Crib y Ddysgl (the third-highest summit in Wales) before the final approach to Yr Wyddfa's trig point — together forming the classic Snowdon Horseshoe when combined with a Pyg or Miners' Track descent.

spots.name: Cadair Idris via the Minffordd Path
spots.description: A challenging but rewarding hike to the summit of Cadair Idris. The Minffordd Path is steep and rugged, with some scrambling sections. The summit offers panoramic views of Cardigan Bay and the surrounding mountains. Legend says you'll either die, go mad, or become a poet if you sleep on the summit!
spots.bestFor: Experienced hikers looking for a challenging climb and stunning views
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners or those with knee problems due to the steep descent.
spots.parking: Minffordd Hotel car park. Pay and display.
spots.insiderTip: Check the weather forecast carefully as conditions can change rapidly on Cadair Idris. The tea room at the Minffordd Hotel is a welcome sight after the hike.
spots.howToDoIt: From the Minffordd car park, the path climbs steeply through oak woodland before opening onto the exposed upper slopes above Llyn Cau — a dramatic corrie lake beneath Craig Cau's cliffs. From here the route scrambles up rough, rocky ground onto the ridge, then follows it to the summit trig point at Penygadair. No technical scrambling skills are required, but the terrain underfoot is loose and uneven throughout, and the exposed sections above Llyn Cau deserve full attention in wind.
spots.access: Public right of way from the Minffordd Hotel car park, which is pay-and-display and the standard start point for this route. No permit needed; the reserve around Llyn Cau is open access.
spots.routeDescription: A horseshoe-shaped route: up through woodland from Minffordd, along the dramatic rim above Llyn Cau's corrie, over Craig Cau, and on to the main summit at Penygadair, with the option to extend along the ridge to Mynydd Moel before dropping back down. The steep, rocky descent back to Minffordd is harder on the knees than the ascent.

spots.name: Cwm Idwal Circular Walk
spots.description: A classic Snowdonia walk around the stunning Cwm Idwal, a glacial cirque with a dark and mysterious atmosphere. The path is mostly well-defined, with some rocky sections. Explore the unique geology and botany of this National Nature Reserve.
spots.bestFor: Families, nature lovers, and those seeking a moderately challenging walk
spots.notSuitableFor: Those with mobility issues due to some rocky terrain.
spots.parking: Ogwen Cottage car park. Pay and display, can get busy.
spots.insiderTip: Bring a picnic and enjoy it by the shores of Llyn Idwal. Look out for the Devil's Kitchen (Twll Du) – a dark cleft in the cliffs above the lake.
spots.howToDoIt: A straightforward waymarked circuit around Llyn Idwal on National Nature Reserve paths — no scrambling or navigation skills required, though there are rocky, uneven sections that need reasonable footing. Follow the path clockwise or anticlockwise from Ogwen Cottage around the lake shore, taking the short detour up toward Twll Du (Devil's Kitchen) if you want a closer look at the cliffs. It's an easy half-day that works well as a warm-up or as a rest day between bigger mountain outings.
spots.access: Cwm Idwal is a National Nature Reserve with open, year-round access and no permit required. Dogs are welcome but must be kept on a lead throughout, as ground-nesting birds and grazing livestock are present. Start point is Ogwen Cottage, a pay-and-display car park that also serves several other routes in this guide and fills quickly on fine days.
spots.routeDescription: A roughly circular walk from Ogwen Cottage around Llyn Idwal, following well-defined NNR paths through classic glacial scenery — hanging valleys, moraines, and the dark cleft of Twll Du (Devil's Kitchen) in the cliffs above. Interpretation boards along the way cover the reserve's unique arctic-alpine plant life, a legacy of the last ice age.

spots.name: Y Garn from Ogwen Cottage
spots.description: A relatively short but steep climb to the summit of Y Garn, offering fantastic views of Tryfan and the Ogwen Valley. The route involves some scrambling over rocky terrain. A good introduction to the Glyderau range.
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners or those uncomfortable with steep ascents and scrambling
spots.parking: Ogwen Cottage car park. Pay and display, fills up quickly.
spots.insiderTip: Extend the walk by continuing along the Glyderau ridge to Glyder Fawr for a more challenging day out.
spots.howToDoIt: From Ogwen Cottage, the path climbs steadily beside the Devil's Kitchen cliffs before cutting up onto Y Garn's flanks, with a rocky, hands-occasionally-needed section as you gain the ridge. Once on top, the summit plateau is broad and the going eases considerably. It's a good next step up from the Cwm Idwal circuit for hikers wanting their first taste of proper Glyderau terrain without committing to a full scramble like Bristly Ridge.
spots.access: Open-access mountain land, no permit required. Starts from the same Ogwen Cottage pay-and-display car park as Cwm Idwal and the Glyderau Horseshoe, which fills quickly — this is one of the busiest trailheads in the park on a fine weekend.
spots.routeDescription: Climbs from Ogwen past the Devil's Kitchen area, then up Y Garn's east ridge to the summit plateau, with views directly across to Tryfan and down into the Ogwen Valley. Can be extended west along the ridge to Glyder Fawr and looped back via the Devil's Kitchen path for a longer, more committing day.

spots.name: Glyderau Bochlwyd Horseshoe
spots.description: The full Glyderau scramble out of the Ogwen Valley — up Bristly Ridge (Grade 1) onto Glyder Fach, across the Cantilever Stone and the shattered tors of Castell y Gwynt to Glyder Fawr, then down past the Devil's Kitchen and Llyn Bochlwyd. A lunar landscape of broken rock that doesn't look like anywhere else in Britain. Proper mountain day with serious scrambling.
spots.bestFor: Confident scramblers wanting the definitive Glyderau day
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners, those with a fear of heights, or in wet/icy/windy conditions
spots.parking: Ogwen Cottage car park. Pay and display, fills very early.
spots.insiderTip: Bristly Ridge is the crux — go up it, not down. If the wet rock looks like glass, bail to the easier Miners' Track variant onto Glyder Fach instead.
spots.howToDoIt: From Ogwen Cottage, walk up to Llyn Bochlwyd before tackling Bristly Ridge — a sustained grade 1 scramble up broken rock steps to Glyder Fach's summit tors. From there it's a rough, boulder-strewn traverse across Castell y Gwynt to Glyder Fawr, then a descent past the Devil's Kitchen back to the valley. This is a full mountain day requiring existing scrambling competence, sound route-finding on ill-defined rocky ground, and a real weather window — it is not a route to learn scrambling on.
spots.access: Open-access mountain land, no permit needed. Starts and finishes at the Ogwen Cottage pay-and-display car park, which fills very early on any settled-weather day; this is one of the most contested trailheads in Snowdonia.
spots.routeDescription: A horseshoe circuit from Ogwen: up via Llyn Bochlwyd and Bristly Ridge onto Glyder Fach, across the shattered rock terrain past the Cantilever Stone and Castell y Gwynt to Glyder Fawr, then down past the Devil's Kitchen cliffs back to the valley floor — a continuously rocky, scrambling-grade circuit with barely a soft step anywhere on it.

spots.name: Moel Siabod via Daear Ddu
spots.description: An overlooked Grade 1 scramble on Moel Siabod's east ridge, starting from Pont Cyfyng near Capel Curig. The Daear Ddu ridge is straightforward when dry but feels exposed; the summit pay-off is one of the best Snowdon Horseshoe views in the park — Crib Goch laid out across the valley like a relief map. Quieter than anything in Ogwen or Llanberis.
spots.bestFor: Hikers ready to start scrambling; anyone after a quieter day with a big-mountain view
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners, anyone uncomfortable with hands-on rock, or in poor visibility
spots.parking: Roadside parking near Pont Cyfyng on the A5. Limited; arrive early.
spots.insiderTip: Descend the gentler western flank back to Pont Cyfyng to make a true circular — coming back down Daear Ddu in the wet is not the move.
spots.howToDoIt: From Pont Cyfyng, climb through forestry onto Moel Siabod's east ridge proper, where Daear Ddu begins — a straightforward grade 1 scramble over rock steps when dry, more serious and best avoided when wet or greasy. The exposure is real but manageable for anyone with some scrambling background; this is often recommended as a step up from Tryfan's North Ridge or Y Garn once you've got a bit more confidence on rock.
spots.access: Open-access mountain land. Roadside parking near Pont Cyfyng on the A5 is limited — a handful of spaces rather than a proper car park — so arriving early matters more here than it does at the bigger trailheads.
spots.routeDescription: Climbs from Pont Cyfyng through forestry onto the Daear Ddu ridge, a rocky scramble gaining the summit of Moel Siabod with a grandstand view across the valley to the entire Snowdon Horseshoe. Descend via the gentler western flank rather than reversing the ridge, looping back down to Pont Cyfyng.

spots.name: Carnedd Llewelyn & Dafydd from Ogwen
spots.description: High-level ridge walk over the second and third highest peaks in Wales (Carnedd Llewelyn 1,064m, Carnedd Dafydd 1,044m). Starts from the A5 at Ogwen, climbs Pen yr Ole Wen — a steep, unrelenting ascent — then follows the broad Carneddau plateau north over Dafydd and Llewelyn before descending via Pen yr Helgi Du. Genuinely remote feeling; you'll see a fraction of the people you would on Snowdon.
spots.bestFor: Experienced mountain hikers seeking solitude and big mileage
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners, anyone weak on navigation, or in poor visibility — the plateau is featureless in cloud
spots.parking: Laybys along the A5 near Ogwen / Llyn Ogwen. Limited.
spots.insiderTip: Pen yr Ole Wen's nose is brutally direct — break it up by traversing in via the eastern ridge from Tal y Llyn Ogwen instead if your knees prefer.
spots.howToDoIt: The standard line climbs Pen yr Ole Wen's steep north nose directly from the A5 — a relentless, unshaded ascent with no easing gradient until the plateau. From there it's sustained high-level walking over Carnedd Dafydd and Carnedd Llewelyn on broad, largely path-free ground, descending via Pen yr Helgi Du's ridge. Good navigation is essential: the summit plateau has few distinguishing features and is genuinely disorientating in cloud, which arrives here more often than on the busier Snowdon massif.
spots.access: Open-access mountain land, no permit required. Parking is limited to laybys along the A5 near Llyn Ogwen — fewer official spaces than at Ogwen Cottage itself, so this stretch of road fills fast too.
spots.routeDescription: A big horseshoe over the Carneddau's two highest summits: a steep, direct climb up Pen yr Ole Wen from the A5, a long traverse across the high plateau over Carnedd Dafydd and Carnedd Llewelyn, then descent via the Pen yr Helgi Du ridge back toward Ogwen — largely trackless, high-level walking with a much more remote feel than the Snowdon or Glyderau routes.

spots.name: Rhinog Fawr
spots.description: A wild and remote mountain with challenging terrain. Rhinog Fawr is known for its ruggedness, steep climbs, and lack of clear paths. Requires good navigation skills and a sense of adventure. Rewards include solitude and stunning views of the coastline.
spots.bestFor: Experienced hikers seeking a challenging and remote adventure
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners, families, or those without good navigation skills.
spots.parking: Small parking area near the Roman Steps. Limited space.
spots.insiderTip: Download an offline map and bring a compass. The terrain is unforgiving and easy to get lost on.
spots.howToDoIt: From Cwm Bychan, follow the ancient Roman Steps path up through the valley before striking out onto Rhinog Fawr's open, largely pathless slopes. There's real navigation required here — heather, boulder fields, and rock outcrops replace any clear trail for long stretches, and route-finding skill matters more than fitness. This is a step up in seriousness from any of the waymarked or well-trodden routes elsewhere in this guide; go with a paper map and compass as backup even if you're carrying GPS.
spots.access: Open-access mountain land. Parking is at the road end in Cwm Bychan, a small car park/campsite with an honesty-box charge, reached via a narrow single-track lane from Llanbedr on the A496 — drive carefully on the blind bends.
spots.routeDescription: Follows the ancient, stone-paved Roman Steps track up through Cwm Bychan before leaving any real path behind on the open, rock-strewn slopes of Rhinog Fawr itself. Rough, remote terrain with sweeping views back to the coast and Cardigan Bay from the summit — one of the wildest, least-engineered routes in this guide.

spots.name: Nantlle Ridge
spots.description: A challenging and rewarding ridge walk with stunning views of Snowdonia and the coast. The Nantlle Ridge involves some scrambling and requires a good head for heights. A less crowded alternative to the more popular ridges.
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners or those with a fear of heights.
spots.parking: Limited parking in the village of Rhyd Ddu or nearby laybys.
spots.insiderTip: Start early to avoid the heat and crowds. The descent from Trum y Ddysgl can be tricky.
spots.howToDoIt: From Rhyd Ddu, climb onto the ridge and follow its full length over a series of tops, with narrow, exposed sections and some easy scrambling required in places, particularly around Trum y Ddysgl. It's a sustained, committing ridge walk rather than a series of discrete summits — once you're on it, the easiest way off is to keep going, so check the full traverse is within your ability and weather window before starting.
spots.access: Open-access mountain land, no permit required. Parking is limited in Rhyd Ddu village and nearby laybys — a modest, informal setup rather than a proper trailhead car park, so options are thin if you arrive late.
spots.routeDescription: A long ridge traverse from Rhyd Ddu across the Nantlle summits, including Y Garn, Mynydd Drws-y-coed, and Trum y Ddysgl, with narrow, airy sections and short scrambling moves throughout. Fewer crowds than the Snowdon or Glyderau ridges for a comparable level of exposure and reward, with views stretching to the coast on a clear day.

spots.name: Aber Falls to Carneddau Foothills
spots.description: A beautiful walk starting at the dramatic Aber Falls, leading into the foothills of the Carneddau range. The route follows well-maintained paths and offers stunning views of the falls and the surrounding mountains. A good option for a less strenuous hike.
spots.bestFor: Families and those looking for a scenic walk with less challenging terrain
spots.notSuitableFor: Those seeking a high mountain adventure
spots.bestSeason: Year-round, but best in spring and summer
spots.parking: Aber Falls car park. Pay and display.
spots.insiderTip: Take a dip in the plunge pool at the base of Aber Falls on a hot day (if you're brave enough!).
spots.howToDoIt: An easy, well-maintained path leads directly from the car park to the base of Aber Falls, suitable for most fitness levels and reasonably sturdy footwear rather than full mountain boots. From the falls, the route continues up into the Carneddau foothills on clearer tracks, giving you the option of a short there-and-back to the waterfall or a longer loop into the hills without committing to a full mountain day.
spots.access: Public right of way throughout, no permit required. The Aber Falls car park is pay-and-display and the standard, well-signed start point for this walk — one of the more straightforward trailheads to find and use in this guide.
spots.routeDescription: A gentle approach from the car park to the dramatic Rhaeadr Fawr (Aber Falls), with the option to extend into the rolling Carneddau foothills beyond on clearer, less demanding tracks than the high-mountain routes elsewhere in this guide — a good low-commitment day, especially with kids or when the tops are in cloud.

spots.name: Welsh 3000s
spots.description: The ultimate Snowdonia hiking challenge: all fifteen Welsh peaks over 3,000ft in a single push. Roughly 30 miles and 13,000ft of ascent, traversing the three big ranges — the Snowdon group (Crib Goch, Crib y Ddysgl, Yr Wyddfa), the Glyderau (Elidir Fawr, Y Garn, Glyder Fawr, Glyder Fach, Tryfan), and the Carneddau (Pen yr Ole Wen, Carnedd Dafydd, Yr Elen, Carnedd Llewelyn, Foel Grach, Garnedd Uchaf, Foel Fras). 24-hour cut-off if you're attempting the classic challenge. Treated by most as a serious mountain undertaking rather than a race.
spots.bestFor: Experienced mountain hikers and ultra-distance walkers wanting Snowdonia's headline challenge
spots.notSuitableFor: Anyone without scrambling experience (Crib Goch and Bristly Ridge are both on the line), shaky navigation, or below-the-ankle fitness for sustained big days
spots.parking: Most attempts start at Pen-y-Pass (Snowdon group first) and finish at Foel Fras / Aber. Logistics typically need a second vehicle or pre-booked pick-up.
spots.insiderTip: Recce each range separately before linking them. The Bwlch Tryfan-to-Pen yr Ole Wen valley crossing is where most attempts fall apart — it's the longest section without a refill point and the unsung crux of the day.
spots.howToDoIt: Most attempts start at Pen-y-Pass, tackle the Snowdon group first (including Crib Goch, so scrambling competence in the dark or in fatigue is a prerequisite, not optional), descend to the Glyderau via Bwlch Tryfan, cross the Ogwen Valley, then finish over the Carneddau to Foel Fras above Aber. This is an ultra-distance mountain day requiring existing scrambling ability, strong navigation, night-hiking experience if going for the 24-hour cut-off, and — critically — a support team or cached supplies, since there's no resupply en route.
spots.access: Open-access mountain land throughout, no permits required for the hills themselves, but logistics are the real access challenge: most parties need a second vehicle or a pre-arranged pick-up at the Foel Fras/Aber end, since it's a linear route roughly 30 miles from the Pen-y-Pass start.
spots.routeDescription: A linear traverse of all fifteen Welsh 3,000-footers: the Snowdon group from Pen-y-Pass (Crib Goch, Crib y Ddysgl, Yr Wyddfa), a descent and re-ascent into the Glyderau (Elidir Fawr, Y Garn, Glyder Fawr, Glyder Fach, Tryfan), then the long valley crossing into the Carneddau for the final seven summits (Pen yr Ole Wen, Carnedd Dafydd, Yr Elen, Carnedd Llewelyn, Foel Grach, Garnedd Uchaf, Foel Fras), finishing with a descent toward Aber.

practicalInfo.weather: Snowdonia's weather is notoriously unpredictable. Conditions can change rapidly, even on seemingly clear days. Be prepared for rain, wind, and mist, especially at higher altitudes. Always check the forecast before setting out and be prepared to turn back if necessary.
gearChecklist: Warm layers (fleece, down jacket) – even in summer, it can get cold at altitude
Hiking boots with good ankle support – essential for the rocky terrain
Navigation equipment (map, compass, GPS) – know how to use them!
Headtorch with spare batteries – even if you're not planning a night hike
Plenty of water and high-energy snacks
Sunscreen and sunglasses – even on cloudy days
Hat and gloves – protect yourself from the elements
Walking poles – helpful for steep ascents and descents

gettingThere.publicTransport: Regular train services to Bangor, Llandudno, and Betws-y-Coed. The Snowdon Sherpa bus service connects the main hiking trailheads.
gettingThere.parkingTips: Parking at popular trailheads can be extremely limited, especially during peak season. Arrive early (before 8am) or use park-and-ride facilities. Consider using public transport to avoid parking hassles.

practicalInfo.safety: Snowdonia is a challenging environment. Plan your route carefully, check the weather forecast, and be prepared for all conditions. Let someone know your planned route and expected return time. In case of emergency, call 999 and ask for Mountain Rescue.

faqs.question: What is the easiest route up Snowdon?
faqs.answer: The Llanberis Path is generally considered the easiest route to the summit of Snowdon. It's the longest but has a gradual incline and a well-maintained path.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to hike Snowdon?
faqs.answer: Hiking Snowdon is free, but you may have to pay for parking at the trailhead. Parking charges typically range from £5 to £15 per day.

faqs.question: What should I wear to hike in Snowdonia?
faqs.answer: Wear waterproof layers, warm layers (fleece, down jacket), hiking boots with good ankle support, and a hat and gloves. The weather in Snowdonia can change rapidly, so be prepared for all conditions.

faqs.question: Can I hike Snowdon in trainers?
faqs.answer: It is NOT recommended to hike Snowdon in trainers, especially on the more challenging routes. Hiking boots with good ankle support are essential for the rocky terrain.

faqs.question: Is Crib Goch dangerous?
faqs.answer: Yes, Crib Goch is a very dangerous route. It's a knife-edge arete with significant exposure and requires excellent scrambling skills and a steady head for heights. It should only be attempted in good weather conditions by experienced mountaineers.

faqs.question: How long does it take to climb Snowdon?
faqs.answer: The time it takes to climb Snowdon varies depending on the route and your fitness level. The Llanberis Path typically takes 5-6 hours round trip, while the Miners' Track and Pyg Track take around 5 hours. Crib Goch as part of the Snowdon Horseshoe takes 5-7 hours.

faqs.question: Are there toilets on Snowdon?
faqs.answer: There are toilet facilities at the summit of Snowdon and at the Hafod Eryri visitor centre, which is usually open from late spring to early autumn. Check opening times before you go.

faqs.question: Are dogs allowed on Snowdon?
faqs.answer: Dogs are allowed on Snowdon, but they must be kept on a lead at all times. Be mindful of other walkers and wildlife. Consider the dog's fitness level and ability to cope with the terrain before attempting a climb.
